system_summary.balanced_overview: Greece has universal eligibility for a core set of health services and health outcomes that are favourable on several OECD indicators, but access and financial protection remain important challenges for many patients.
system_summary.public_system_role: Public coverage is effectively universal for core services, while private spending and private providers also play a substantial role.

facts.claim: All of the population in Greece is covered for a core set of services.
facts.source_name: OECD Health at a Glance 2025: Greece

facts.claim: Life expectancy in Greece was above the OECD average in the 2025 country note.
facts.source_name: OECD Health at a Glance 2025: Greece

facts.claim: Only 27% of people in Greece reported being satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare, versus an OECD average of 64%.
facts.source_name: OECD Health at a Glance 2025: Greece

facts.claim: Mandatory prepayment covered 61% of health spending in Greece, compared with an OECD average of 75%.
facts.source_name: OECD Health at a Glance 2025: Greece

facts.claim: The OECD comparable indicator reported unmet medical-care needs for 12.1% of people in Greece, versus 3.4% across the OECD countries with comparable data.
facts.denominator_note: OECD comparable population indicator; do not combine directly with the EU-SILC 'among those expressing a need' figure.

facts.claim: Among people in Greece who expressed a need for healthcare, 21.9% reported unmet needs due to cost, distance or waiting times.
facts.denominator_note: EU-SILC subgroup who expressed a healthcare need; this denominator differs from the OECD comparable population indicator.
facts.source_name: Greece: Country Health Profile 2025 (OECD/European Observatory/European Commission)

facts.claim: Out-of-pocket payments accounted for 34% of current health expenditure in Greece in 2023, almost double the EU average according to the 2025 Country Health Profile.
Public coverage of dental care in Greece is very limited in practice, with most dental care paid out of pocket.
Unmet medical-care needs due to waiting times have increased in Greece since 2019; Greece introduced the Unified Digital List of Surgeries in 2024 to centralise public-hospital surgery waiting lists.

selling_boundary: Do not say the Greek public system is 'bad' or unsafe.
Acknowledge universal core-service eligibility and favourable health outcomes before discussing access constraints.
Frame IPMI as an option for private choice, portability, wider networks, predictable financial protection and cross-border access—not as a replacement for emergency/public-health infrastructure.
Do not imply that private insurance guarantees shorter waits for every treatment or every provider.
Use public-system statistics only with year and source context.

oop_interpretation.correct_meaning: Out-of-pocket (OOP) expenditure means healthcare spending paid directly by households at the point of use where public or private third-party financing does not pay the full amount. It includes co-payments and direct household payments.
not_proven_by_metric: It does not by itself show that the patient was uninsured.
It does not by itself show that a local private insurer rejected or failed to pay a claim.

It does not identify whether each payment related to a public-system gap, an insurance exclusion/sublimit, a co-payment, an uncovered service, a private-provider choice, pharmaceuticals, dental care or other direct spending.

greece_2023_oop_distribution.interpretation: The high inpatient component is relevant evidence that households directly finance a substantial amount of hospital care, but it still cannot be attributed specifically to private-insurance denials or uninsured status.

insurance_argumentation.objective: When authoritative evidence shows access constraints, waiting-time pressure, high unmet needs or substantial household out-of-pocket spending, HAL should explain how private health insurance can mitigate those practical risks for people who can afford private cover.
balanced_structure: Start by acknowledging the essential social role of the public healthcare system.

Recognise that public healthcare is particularly important for economically vulnerable people, people without private insurance, and patients whose conditions may not be fully insurable under private underwriting.
Then identify the specific access or financial-protection problem shown by the evidence, with year/source context.
Translate the statistic into a practical insurance consequence: waiting for elective care, paying directly for treatment, restricted provider choice, or uncertainty about access.

Explain how a suitable private health plan may reduce that problem through private-provider access, broader choice, direct billing, predictable insured limits or faster access where private capacity is available.
For affluent/HNWI clients, explain the additional value of IPMI: international provider choice, cross-border treatment, portability, higher limits and comprehensive service.
Never claim that private insurance eliminates all waiting, covers every condition, or replaces the public system.

waiting_lists.instruction: Waiting times should be treated as a major decision factor when supported by current country-specific evidence. Do not merely mention them in passing. Explain that long waits for consultations, diagnostics or elective procedures can be a material reason for someone who can afford it to seek private cover.
waiting_lists.boundary: Do not say that every public hospital or every specialty has long waits, and do not promise that every private provider is immediately available.

evidence_to_argument_examples.evidence: Low satisfaction with availability of quality healthcare
evidence_to_argument_examples.insurance_argument: A low satisfaction rate can indicate that access, availability or user experience does not consistently meet expectations. For clients who value control and choice, private insurance can provide an alternative route into private care.

A high unmet-needs rate suggests that some people who need care face barriers such as cost, distance or waiting. A well-designed private plan may reduce some of these barriers by funding access to private providers and broader networks.

High household direct spending means patients finance a substantial share of care themselves. Private insurance can improve financial predictability by transferring eligible medical costs to the insurer, subject to policy limits, excesses, exclusions and underwriting.

Where public waiting times are material, private insurance can be valuable because it may allow access to private consultations, diagnostics and elective treatment without relying exclusively on the public queue.

tone: Support private insurance when the evidence and client profile justify it.
Do not demean public doctors, hospitals or the social role of the public system.
Do not present private care as clinically superior by default; focus on access, choice, timing, financial protection and continuity.
